newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr buried beneath yen steamroller.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr buried beneath yen steamroller.

text.p: The Australian dollar was left to bump around in a narrow range on the U.S. currency at midday as market expended all its energy in wild cross trading.

The session was dominated by huge Japanese flows into the yen as last week's breakdown of the U.S. dollar triggered fears its two year uptrend had come to an end and investors clambered to cut long positions. Panic selling saw US$/yen plunge to 117.60 at one stage -- against a NY close of 120.20 -- before a calming word from Japanese officials forced a squeeze to 118.50.
The local dollar was buried in the fallout, losing three yen at one point to 91.30 before steadying just atop 92.00.
By 12.15 pm (2215 GMT) the dollar was keeping a low profile at US$0.7763/68 having drifted from an early US$0.7759/64 and US$0.7782/87 late here Friday.

Immediate support had been found at US$0.7755, with further bulwarks put at US$0.7735 and US$0.7720, while resistance had made itself felt at US$0.7795 and US$0.7810, with US$0.7860 looking a distant bull target now.

The action was much more savage on the crosses where the currency was barely holding its own at 92.00/10 yen having fled from 95.64/74 late here Friday and 99.00 this time last Monday -- making an eight percent fall in a week.

The resurgence in the yen reflected a number of factors, not least of which was that the whole world had been short yen/long dollars for a very long time. Investors were understandably nervous, therefore, when the U.S. dollar's rally seemed to have run out of puff in April.

Perhaps sensing the change in mood, Japanese officials hardened their verbal campaign in support of a firmer yen -- with targets such as 103.00 yen bandied about. They were aided by signs of recovery in both the economy and the stock market which stirred long dormant thoughts about the inevitable day when Japanese interest rates are raised from their record lows.
Most analysts reckoned the talk premature, but Japanese bond yields rose regardless.

Even then the damage might not have been great given both the local and U.S. dollars offered yields far above those in Japan, but it was at this moment the market began to question its conviction the Federal Reserve would soon be raising rates.

The market has long been discounting a 0.25 point hike in the funds rate at the Fed's May 20 meeting but detected enough ambivalence -- whether real or imaginary is beside the point -- in a speech by chairman Alan Greenspan on Friday to raise the spectre of a narrowing in US$/yen interest differentials.
This had important implications for the A$ since it the Japanese hunger for higher yields had played a major part in its rousing recovery from a 60.00 yen trough in June 1995.
Indeed, the issuance of yen/A$ samurai bonds had picked up in recent weeks showing that demand was still there.

Ironically, the growth may have hurt the dollarsince the Tokyo securities houses which handled the bonds were believed to be among the leading AUD/yen sellers as they sought to cut all dollar exposure. Longer term, analysts felt Australian yields would still be high enough to attract some Japanese demand, but probably not on the scale seen in the recent past.
With so much happening on the crosses the market largely ignored a soft set of domestic housing and prices data.

Housing finance commitments for March fell 1.3 percent when forecasts had favoured a 1.0 percent rise, leaving the trend negative for the last four months. In contrast the value of commitments rose 1.5 percent on the month and was at historically high levels.
Manufacturing output prices for March confirmed the lack of inflationary pressures by falling 0.1 percent on the back of a drop in car and petrol prices.
